all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: head-mounted display
concepts.definition: A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.

defining_facts.text: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors.
In 1961, engineers at Philco Corporation developed an early head-mounted display (HMD) that could track users' motion but was bulky and uncomfortable to wear.
In 1965, Tom Furness and colleagues at the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base worked on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays (HMDs).
In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

In 1985, Scott Fisher and colleagues at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) developed and launched Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED), the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display (HMD) with a wide field of view.

The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.
Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.
A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.

A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.
Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

concepts.name: virtual environment
concepts.definition: Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

defining_facts.text: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

The artificial or synthetic environment of a virtual reality (VR) system is a computer-generated graphical representation of a real world or an imaginary or fantastic world, populated with artificial objects, and is not a real environment.

An artificial environment in a virtual reality (VR) system can recreate a real world using real-world imagery or video, as in a virtual tour, but it still counts as a virtual reality system because it is a computer-generated scenario and changes are not happening in real time.

The sensory experience characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes and ears, so the user can immersively experience the artificial or synthetic environment, and this immersive experience is a hallmark of a virtual reality system.

The user interaction characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system must be interactive: the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens in the environment, producing dynamic changes in the virtual environment, just as people interact with objects in the real world.

concepts.name: immersive experience
concepts.definition: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.

defining_facts.text: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

concepts.name: interaction
concepts.definition: Interaction is the activity that takes place between a user and a system, often by manipulating an image or parts of it with input devices. In immersive environments it is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and system control.

defining_facts.text: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.
Interaction in non-immersive settings, such as augmented reality (AR), is similar to familiar interactions such as touch and gesture.

For immersive virtual reality (VR) or mixed reality (MR) experiences, specialized techniques and setups are used, and suitable interaction techniques should be known and used to design the experience properly and enhance presence.

Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.

In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen.

The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation.

concepts.name: augmented reality system
concepts.definition: An Augmented reality system is a system with four required characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content registered in 3D, that content is experienced through the user's sensory organs, and it supports real-time interaction with that content in the enhanced environment.

defining_facts.text: The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

An augmented reality (AR) system has four characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content such as image, video, or text; the enhancement is registered in 3D so that it appears at its appropriate place rather than randomly and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects; the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs; and the system supports the user's interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times.

A system is identified as an augmented reality (AR) system by checking the four AR characteristics one by one, and it is an AR system only if all four are satisfied; if at least one characteristic is not satisfied, it is not an AR system.

concepts.name: tracked handheld controller
concepts.definition: Tracked handheld controller is a virtual reality hand input device that has six degrees of freedom tracking, allowing the system to track its movements.

defining_facts.text: Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs.

Tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices with six degrees of freedom tracking, so the system can track their movements; input controllers that come with modern virtual reality (VR) systems are tracked devices so that break-in presence is avoided, and VIVE controllers are an example because they combine a joystick with tracking and are mainly used in VR.

Tracked handheld controllers have the limitation that users cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction because the user's hands are occupied with the controller, although force feedback controllers may sometimes resolve the issue.

concepts.name: ray
concepts.definition: A ray is a trajectory or path in the ray view of light that is assumed to be the trace of the motion of a single hypothetical photon.

defining_facts.text: The ray view of light describes light as rays, which are trajectories or paths assumed to be traces of the motion of a single hypothetical photon, and it is helpful for explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility.

concepts.name: cone
concepts.definition: Cone is a photoreceptor in the human eye, mainly located in the fovea, the central region of the retina, that is used for photopic vision, in which color is perceived, and is served by approximately one optic nerve fiber, which aids image acuity.

defining_facts.text: The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea.
Multiple rods can share a single optic nerve fiber, which aids sensitivity to lower levels of light, whereas approximately one optic nerve fiber serves each cone, which aids image acuity.

Vision accomplished only with cones is photopic vision, which is more related to direct or central vision, and vision accomplished only with rods is scotopic vision, which is more related to peripheral vision.

Color is perceived only in photopic vision, which is accomplished with cones and gives a sense of color, whereas in scotopic vision weak lights are perceived as a series of grays and color perception is not that good.

concepts.name: degree of freedom
concepts.definition: Degree of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space; in 3D space, an object can have six degrees of freedom: three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes, and three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch.

defining_facts.text: The concept of degrees of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space.

In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.
In a virtual world, motion is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.

concepts.name: six degrees of freedom
concepts.definition: Six degrees of freedom is the total of six freedoms an object can have in three-dimensional space, consisting of three rotational freedoms called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational freedoms along the x, y, and z axes.

defining_facts.text: In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.

concepts.name: object interaction
concepts.definition: Object interaction is a kind of interaction in immersive virtual environments that involves selecting one or more virtual objects in the environment and manipulating a selected object to change its properties.

defining_facts.text: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.

In any virtual experience, object interaction is broadly of two types: selection, which specifies one or more objects from a set of virtual objects in the virtual world, and manipulation, which interacts with a selected object to change its properties; the two types mostly have separate interaction techniques.

concepts.name: navigation
concepts.definition: Navigation is an interaction in an immersive virtual world that moves the user from one point to another by changing the user's viewpoint, mostly without object interaction, and has two components: locomotion and wayfinding.

defining_facts.text: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.
The goal of navigation in a virtual world is to move the user from one point to another, which means a change of the user's field of view or viewpoint.
The movement involved in navigation in a virtual world has two parts: the travel part and the wayfinding part.
Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.

never_defined.name: virtual object
never_defined.definition: A virtual object is an object that does not exist in the real world and can be seen in a virtual world or added to the real world so that it appears to coexist with real objects.

never_defined.name: handheld controller
never_defined.definition: A handheld controller is an input device held by the user, used in non-immersive VR, and an example of a self-grounded haptic device.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional
never_defined.definition: Three-dimensional (3D) is used to describe registered augmented reality enhancements, selectable regions of virtual space, and games or interactive content.

never_defined.name: interaction technique
never_defined.definition: An interaction technique is a method used in virtual reality to select or manipulate virtual objects, navigate a virtual world, or issue system-control commands.

never_defined.name: orientation
never_defined.definition: Orientation is a part of pose, together with position, that is tracked or estimated for a user, sensor, or head, and modified for an object.

never_defined.name: controller
never_defined.definition: A controller is virtual reality hardware that a user operates to extend a ray for selection and to control navigation.

never_defined.name: gesture
never_defined.definition: A gesture is a hand movement or signal that a user provides to a system, and the system detects and translates the gesture into a command or object selection.

never_defined.name: controller-based interaction
never_defined.definition: Controller-based interaction is a method of implementing hand manipulation that uses a controller, such as a joystick-based controller.

never_defined.name: eye gaze
never_defined.definition: Eye gaze is input captured by non-hand-based input devices and can be used for pointing-based selection when hand tracking is unavailable.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional scene
never_defined.definition: A three-dimensional scene is a scene in a three-dimensional world coordinate system from which a portion is selected and projected onto a two-dimensional display.

never_defined.name: hand gesture
never_defined.definition: Hand gesture is a user hand motion used for interaction or to indicate that manipulation is done.

never_defined.name: head position
never_defined.definition: Head position is the position of a user's head that a head tracker estimates and from which a virtual ray is extended for head pointing when hand tracking is unavailable.

never_defined.name: hand tracking
never_defined.definition: Hand tracking is a form of tracking, for example in augmented reality application development, that allows a virtual ray in pointing-based selection to be attached to a virtual hand.

never_defined.name: size
never_defined.definition: Size is a property of virtual objects or a measure of virtual reality applications, appearing in perception, object selection, modeling, and storage optimization.

never_defined.name: distance
never_defined.definition: Distance is a variable in XR that gives how far an object is from a viewpoint or camera position, how far directly connected nodes are apart, or how far a light source is from a surface point.

never_defined.name: direction
never_defined.definition: Direction is the orientation of a sound source, an object to be selected, or user movement in two- or three-dimensional space, used to describe sound-source location, support object selection, and support wayfinding.

never_defined.name: shape
never_defined.definition: Shape is a geometric property of an object that haptic exploration can infer and shearing can change.

never_defined.name: smart glove
never_defined.definition: A smart glove is a force feedback device used in XR to provide touch sensation and to implement hand manipulation.

never_defined.name: object selection technique
never_defined.definition: An Object selection technique is a technique in a virtual world for selecting objects, and its kinds include hand, pointing-based, image plane, volume-based, and bimanual selection.

never_defined.name: selection performance
never_defined.definition: Selection performance is the performance of a user while accomplishing an object selection task in a virtual experience, and a suitable object selection technique is chosen so that it is maximized.

never_defined.name: selection task
never_defined.definition: A selection task is a task in a virtual experience, and user performance while accomplishing the selection task is influenced by variables such as the distance, direction, and size of the object to be selected, object density, and number of targets.

never_defined.name: density
never_defined.definition: Density is one of the parameters that influence user performance in a virtual object selection task, including the density of objects around the target object.

never_defined.name: target object
never_defined.definition: A target object is an object to be selected in an object selection task in a virtual experience.

never_defined.name: number of targets
never_defined.definition: The number of targets is a variable used to determine the kind of object selection technique that is suitable in a virtual experience, so that selection performance is maximized.

never_defined.name: selection with the hand
never_defined.definition: Selection with the hand is one of the object selection techniques in a virtual world.

never_defined.name: bimanual selection
never_defined.definition: Bimanual selection is one of the object selection techniques in a virtual world.

never_defined.name: grab
never_defined.definition: Grab is part of a hand selection technique that selects virtual objects in a virtual world by having the user directly reach out to virtually touch the object.

never_defined.name: one-to-one mapping
never_defined.definition: One-to-one mapping is a mapping of a physical hand's motion and orientation to a virtual hand, tying the virtual hand to the physical hand and allowing natural hand movements.

never_defined.name: hand velocity
never_defined.definition: Hand velocity is the speed of the user's physical hand, used to decide when the virtual hand remains still in the prism technique.

never_defined.name: grabbing technique
never_defined.definition: Grabbing technique is a hand selection technique such as intent-driven selection.

never_defined.name: eye-gaze pointing
never_defined.definition: Eye-gaze pointing is a pointing method for pointing-based selection that uses an eye tracker.

never_defined.name: eye tracker
never_defined.definition: An eye tracker is used for eye-gaze pointing for pointing-based selection.

never_defined.name: selectable object
never_defined.definition: A selectable object is an object in bend cast whose point-line distance from a ray is calculated to detect the closest object.

never_defined.name: point-line distance
never_defined.definition: Point-line distance is a distance calculated from each selectable object to detect the closest selectable object in bend cast.

never_defined.name: depth marker
never_defined.definition: A depth marker is a user-controlled marker, positioned by moving the hand forward or backward, that disambiguates multiple intersected objects and selects the object intersected by the pointing vector and closest to the marker.

never_defined.name: two-dimensional
never_defined.definition: Two-dimensional (2D) is used to describe selection techniques, image planes, and games or interactive content.

never_defined.name: image plane
never_defined.definition: Image plane is a two-dimensional image in which a user positions fingers or hands to surround or enclose an object.

never_defined.name: box
never_defined.definition: A box is a three-dimensional region in volumetric selection, usually a cube but possibly a rectangular parallelepiped, that a user positions, orients, and progressively reduces to select objects in virtual space.

never_defined.name: cube
never_defined.definition: A cube is a primitive object type that can be created directly in Unity and can be a three-dimensional region used in volumetric selection in virtual space.

never_defined.name: sphere
never_defined.definition: A sphere is one of the possible 3D regions for volumetric selection of objects and a primitive object type that can be created in Unity.

never_defined.name: bimanual
never_defined.definition: Bimanual is a kind of volumetric selection technique in which the user uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box to select a region of three-dimensional space.

never_defined.name: rectangular parallelepiped
never_defined.definition: A rectangular parallelepiped is a possible shape of the box used in a two-handed box selection technique for selecting a region of three-dimensional space.

never_defined.name: scale
never_defined.definition: Scale is one of an object's properties; in a game object, its transform stores scale with position and rotation, and scale can be modified during object manipulation.

never_defined.name: behavior
never_defined.definition: Behavior is one of the properties of an object that can be modified during object manipulation.

never_defined.name: manipulation technique
never_defined.definition: Manipulation technique is a technique that includes hand manipulation, indirect manipulation, bimanual manipulation, and integrated hybrid manipulation.

never_defined.name: bimanual manipulation
never_defined.definition: Bimanual manipulation is a manipulation technique.

never_defined.name: integrated hybrid manipulation
never_defined.definition: Integrated hybrid manipulation is one of the manipulation techniques.

never_defined.name: hand selection
never_defined.definition: Hand selection is what precedes hand manipulation.

never_defined.name: gesture-based manipulation
never_defined.definition: Gesture-based manipulation is a way of implementing hand manipulation, which follows hand selection and is used to manipulate objects.

never_defined.name: computational power
never_defined.definition: Computational power is required for hand manipulation, which needs somewhat more of it or specialized devices that may be relatively costly.

never_defined.name: local proxy
never_defined.definition: A local proxy is a proxy that a user manipulates, such as a physical proxy prop linked to a neurological data set, so that moving the local proxy moves a linked virtual object in a virtual world.

never_defined.name: physical proxy prop
never_defined.definition: A physical proxy prop is a local proxy in an indirect manipulation technique, linked to a neurological data set, so moving it moves a linked virtual object in a virtual world.

never_defined.name: neurological data set
never_defined.definition: A neurological data set is a data set linked to a physical proxy prop that is used as a local proxy in an indirect manipulation technique.

never_defined.name: miniature model
never_defined.definition: Miniature model is a handheld model of a virtual environment that represents all objects in the environment, so manipulating an object in the miniature model manipulates the corresponding object in the virtual environment.

never_defined.name: imaginary axis
never_defined.definition: An imaginary axis is an axis used in bimanual manipulation techniques, on both sides of which two handheld controllers may be placed symmetrically.

never_defined.name: virtual spindle
never_defined.definition: A Virtual spindle is a virtual object defined by two handheld controllers with six degrees of freedom, placed symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis and moved simultaneously.

never_defined.name: virtual world object
never_defined.definition: Virtual world object is an object in a virtual world that, in the spindle technique, can be moved and rotated simultaneously by moving both hands in unison.
